title: “TOUCH NOT MY ANOINTED” — THE VERSE THAT WAS NEVER MEANT TO SILENCE YOU
paragraphs: “TOUCH NOT MY ANOINTED” — THE VERSE THAT WAS NEVER MEANT TO SILENCE YOU
What if one of the Bible verses you were taught to fear was never saying what you were told it said?
Maybe you have heard it from a pulpit.
Maybe someone whispered it after you asked an uncomfortable question.

Maybe you watched something happen in a church that did not seem right. Money disappeared without explanation. A leader behaved in a way that troubled your conscience. Someone was wounded. Someone finally spoke. Someone asked for accountability.
And suddenly four words entered the room like a spiritual threat:
“Touch not Mine anointed.”
Conversation over.
Questions became rebellion.
Discernment became dishonor.
Accountability became persecution.
And somewhere inside you, fear whispered, “What if questioning this person means I am questioning God?”
But what if that fear came from a verse removed from its context?
What if Psalm 105:15 was never given to make Christian leaders untouchable?
And what if reading the words surrounding it changes the entire conversation?
The King James Version reads:
“Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.” — Psalm 105:15
Those words are Scripture. They are holy. They should not be mocked, dismissed, or explained away.
But because they are Scripture, we must care enough about them to ask what God actually meant.
The Hebrew is striking:
אַל־תִּגְּעוּ בִמְשִׁיחָי וְלִנְבִיאַי אַל־תָּרֵעוּ
’Al-tigge‘u vimshichai, velinvi’ai ’al-tare‘u.
In straightforward English:
“Do not touch My anointed ones, and do My prophets no harm.”
Notice something easily missed.
“Anointed” is plural.
בִמְשִׁיחָי — vimshichai — “My anointed ones.”
The underlying word is related to מָשִׁיחַ, mashiach, “anointed one,” the word from which we get “Messiah.”
But Psalm 105 is not describing a modern preacher standing behind a pulpit and warning people not to question him.
Read backward.
That is where the walls begin to move.

The psalm remembers God’s covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It speaks about people who were few in number, strangers and sojourners, wandering from nation to nation and from kingdom to kingdom. God protected them and rebuked kings on their behalf.
Then comes the famous declaration:
“Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.”

The “anointed ones” in this immediate context are the patriarchal covenant family God was preserving—particularly Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—not a special class of modern Christian leaders who have been granted immunity from examination.
That changes everything.
The verse so often used by powerful people to protect themselves originally appears in a song celebrating God protecting vulnerable covenant people as they wandered among powerful kings.
Sit with that.
A text about God protecting His servants from powerful rulers can become dangerously distorted when powerful religious figures use it to protect themselves from legitimate accountability.
That is not a small interpretive mistake.
It can turn comfort into intimidation.
It can turn Scripture into a shield for human power.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You were not trying to destroy the church.
You were trying to understand what happened.
You were not trying to dishonor God.
You were trying to reconcile what you saw with what Scripture says.
You were told not to gossip—and rightly so.
But eventually “gossip” seemed to mean anything that made leadership uncomfortable.
You were told to honor spiritual authority—and Christians absolutely should honor faithful leadership.
But eventually “honor” seemed to mean silence.
You were told, “David would not touch Saul.”
And that story deserves to be taken seriously too.
Saul really was the LORD’s anointed king.
David really did refuse to kill him.
When David had an opportunity to strike Saul, he refused to “put forth” his hand against the LORD’s anointed.
But notice what David did not do.
David did not pretend Saul was behaving righteously.
David did not surrender himself to Saul so Saul could murder him.
David did not call Saul’s persecution acceptable because Saul held an anointed office.
David spared Saul’s life while still confronting Saul with the truth.
He essentially said: Look at what you are doing. I have not sinned against you, yet you are hunting me to take my life. Let the LORD judge between us.
That is a world away from saying, “A spiritual leader must never be questioned.”
David refused vengeance.
He did not refuse discernment.
He refused murder.
He did not deny wrongdoing.
He honored the office without pretending the man occupying it could do no wrong.
There is a lesson there for both wounded church members and angry critics.
Biblical accountability is not permission for a mob.
Christians must not confuse legitimate correction with gossip, slander, character assassination, rumor, online humiliation, or the thrill of watching somebody fall.
A pastor is not fair game simply because he is visible.
An accusation is not automatically true because it is dramatic.
A viral post is not evidence.
A suspicion is not a conviction.
Scripture protects leaders from reckless accusations too.
Paul tells Timothy:
“Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses.” — 1 Timothy 5:19
That should make us careful.
But keep reading.
The next verse says:
“Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear.” — 1 Timothy 5:20
There it is.
Both truths standing beside each other.
Do not casually receive accusations against an elder.
And when sin is established and persists, leadership is not exempt from correction.
Scripture protects faithful leaders from slander without protecting sinful leaders from accountability.
The Bible refuses both extremes.
It will not give us permission to destroy pastors with unverified accusations.
And it will not give pastors permission to use their position to escape biblical accountability.
That balance matters because Jesus loves His church too much for either abuse.
This is where the issue becomes painfully personal.
Because spiritual abuse often does not begin with somebody announcing, “I intend to manipulate you.”
It can begin with biblical language.
“Honor.”
“Submission.”
“Authority.”
“Covering.”
“Rebellion.”
“Anointing.”
Words that may contain legitimate biblical ideas can become dangerous when detached from the rest of Scripture and placed into the hands of someone who refuses correction.
And there is a devastating irony here.
A leader may quote “Touch not Mine anointed” to defend himself while forgetting that Scripture repeatedly records God Himself confronting leaders.
Nathan confronted David.
David was king.
David was anointed.
David was also guilty.
Nathan did not walk into the throne room and say, “Because you are anointed, adultery and bloodshed are none of my business.”
He said:
“Thou art the man.”
And David eventually said:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
That is what godly leadership looks like when confronted by truth—not perfection, but repentance.
The truly terrifying sign is not merely that a Christian leader can sin.
Every Christian leader is still a sinner dependent upon grace.
The terrifying sign is when someone begins acting as though his calling places him beyond correction.
Because the Gospel never creates untouchable celebrities.
It creates servants.
Jesus Himself overturned the worldly model of leadership.
The rulers of the Gentiles exercise dominion over people, He taught His disciples, but “it shall not be so among you.” Greatness in His kingdom looks like service.
Then look at Christ.
The One who actually possessed all authority washed feet.
The One before whom angels worship did not need manipulation to preserve His importance.
The King wore a towel.
Then He wore thorns.
Then He carried a cross.
That is Christian authority.
Not “How dare you question me?”
But “How can I serve?”
Not “Protect my reputation at all costs.”
But “Christ must be honored at all costs.”
Not “I am too anointed to repent.”
But “Search me, O God.”
And perhaps the most sobering part is that Jesus Christ is the Anointed One in the ultimate messianic sense.
Χριστός — Christos.
Christ.
The Anointed One.
The Messiah.
Christianity was never supposed to revolve around protecting the personal kingdoms of charismatic personalities.
It revolves around Jesus.
The pastor did not die for you.
The apostle did not die for you.
The prophet did not die for you.
The denomination did not die for you.
The ministry brand did not shed its blood for you.
Jesus Christ did.
There is only one name before which every knee will ultimately bow.
Jesus.
And when a ministry begins making people more afraid of questioning a human leader than of disobeying Christ, something has gone terribly wrong.
But there is another side to this article, and it may hurt differently.
Perhaps you have used legitimate concerns as permission for bitterness.
Perhaps somebody wounded you in church, and slowly your pain became contempt for the entire body of Christ.
Perhaps “discernment” became the respectable Christian word you used for constantly searching for somebody to expose.
Perhaps you enjoy watching ministers fall.
Perhaps you share accusations before checking whether they are true.
Perhaps you have spoken about servants of God in ways you would never want others to speak about you.
Then this article is not permission to continue.
Jesus calls you to repentance too.
Truth without love becomes cruelty.
Love without truth becomes sentimentality.
Biblical Christianity permits neither.
We do not protect wolves by silencing sheep.
But neither do we become wolves while claiming to protect sheep.
We tell the truth.
We seek evidence.
We reject gossip.
We protect the vulnerable.
We honor faithful shepherds.
We confront proven sin biblically.
We forgive where repentance is real.
We refuse vengeance.
And above everything else, we remain under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Because the answer to abusive authority is not rebellion against all authority.
The answer is Christlike authority.
The answer to spiritual manipulation is not abandoning Scripture.
The answer is reading Scripture faithfully.
The answer to a distorted gospel is not no gospel.
It is the true Gospel.
And this is where scandal meets grace.
David, the man who refused to kill Saul, later became the king confronted for his own horrifying sin.
Think about that.
The man who once respected another anointed king eventually became an anointed king who needed someone courageous enough to confront him.
That alone should destroy our appetite for simplistic categories.
Today you may be David hiding from Saul.
Tomorrow you may be David standing before Nathan.
Sometimes you are the wounded person who needs protection.
Sometimes you are the sinner who needs confrontation.
Sometimes you need courage to speak.
Sometimes you need humility to listen.
Every one of us desperately needs Jesus.
That is why grace is not pretending sin never happened.
Grace tells the truth about sin and then points trembling sinners toward a Savior whose blood is greater than their shame.
The cross does not say sin does not matter.
The cross proves sin matters so much that the Son of God gave Himself to save sinners from it.
Jesus does not merely expose darkness.
He calls people out of it.
He does not merely uncover scandal.
He offers grace.
He does not merely say, “You are guilty.”
To the repentant sinner He offers forgiveness, cleansing, restoration, and a completely new identity in Him.
So if you are a pastor reading this, do not fear biblical accountability.
Fear becoming the kind of leader who no longer believes he needs it.
Surround yourself with people who love Jesus more than they love your approval.
Give them permission to tell you the truth.
Do not build a throne where Christ placed a cross.
If you are a church member reading this, honor your leaders.
Pray for them.
Do not spread rumors.
Do not confuse disagreement with abuse.
Do not weaponize accusations.
But never surrender your conscience to a human being.
Test teaching by Scripture.
Christ alone is Lord of the conscience.
And if you have been spiritually wounded, hear this carefully:
You do not have to choose between truth and Jesus.
Jesus is the truth.
What somebody did while carrying a Bible does not redefine the Bible.
What somebody did while standing behind a pulpit does not redefine Christ.
What somebody did in the name of God does not change the character of God.
Do not let the person who wounded you steal Jesus from you too.
Bring the wound to Him.
Bring the anger.
Bring the confusion.
Bring the questions you were told you were not allowed to ask.
Bring the bitterness you are embarrassed to admit.
Bring everything into the light.
And then look at the cross.
There hangs the true Anointed One.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Wounded.
Crucified.
Not exploiting sheep but dying for them.
Not demanding that others bleed to preserve His kingdom but shedding His own blood to bring sinners into His kingdom.
That is your Shepherd.
That is your King.
That is Jesus.
Maybe you came into this article angry at a pastor.
Maybe you came here defending one.
Maybe you came here because somebody sent this to you and you were ready to argue.
But perhaps the Holy Spirit has turned the mirror around.
Because eventually this stops being about “them.”
What do you do when Scripture corrects you?
Can you repent?
Can you forgive?
Can you admit you were wrong?
Can you refuse revenge when somebody really has wronged you?
Can you honor faithful leadership without idolizing it?
Can you expose darkness without enjoying another person's destruction?
Can you follow Jesus when doing so costs you your pride?
That is the deeper test.
And maybe your next prayer needs to be very simple:

“Jesus, show me where I have believed people more than Your Word. Show me where I have confused honor with fear, discernment with bitterness, loyalty with idolatry, or accountability with revenge. Forgive me. Heal what has been wounded. Expose what needs to be exposed in me. Teach me to love truth without losing love. I belong to You.”
If this uncovered something you have been afraid to admit, do not hide behind religious language.
Someone reading the comments may discover they are not alone.
And if you know a believer who has been frightened into silence by a verse taken out of context, send this to them personally.
Save it too.
Because eventually somebody may quote those four words again, and you will want to remember the verses surrounding them.

Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is nothing more than religious power to follow as well. Let them encounter the Jesus who confronts sin while opening His arms to sinners.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves that you love Jesus. It does not.
And never because anyone should manipulate you into believing God will be disappointed with you if you cannot financially support a ministry.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ.

But one practical way believers who are able can participate in spreading biblical teaching is by supporting ministries whose work they prayerfully believe is bearing faithful fruit. Your sharing matters too.
You belong to Jesus before you belong to any ministry.
Follow Christ before personalities.
Know Scripture beyond quotations.
Honor godly leaders without worshiping them.
Refuse slander without surrendering discernment.
Protect the wounded without becoming consumed by vengeance.
And when scandal reveals how broken human beings can become—even inside churches—run toward the Savior whose grace is powerful enough to expose sin without abandoning the repentant sinner.
Because perhaps the most dangerous misuse of “Touch not Mine anointed” is not simply misunderstanding an ancient verse.
It is allowing a human voice to become so powerful that you become afraid to hear what God actually said.
So open the Bible.
Read before the verse.
Read after the verse.
Look at Jesus.
And never again confuse protecting someone's platform with protecting the Gospel.
The Gospel does not need an untouchable man.
It already has an unconquerable Christ.
And please, do not leave without answering the question Scripture has quietly placed before all of us:
When truth finally reaches your door, will you protect your image—or will you let Jesus rewrite your story?
Because the hands pierced for you are the only hands worthy of holding the throne of your heart.
